title: Cloud ML Platforms
blurb: Tests how the open-source pieces built earlier map onto SageMaker and Bedrock, why S3 matters for lock-in, what each managed service replaces, the costs that catch people out, and how a Solutions Architect checks for hard constraints before weighing the rest.

questions.prompt: Which SageMaker service is the managed version of Chapter 25's hand-rolled drift checks?
options: Model Monitor
Processing Jobs
Pipelines
Feature Store
questions.explanation: The chapter maps hand-rolled drift checks to SageMaker Model Monitor. Feature Store addresses training and serving skew. Processing Jobs run data preparation. Pipelines orchestrates CI/CD steps.

questions.prompt: How are SageMaker Training Jobs billed?
options: A flat monthly fee per user
Per model version registered
Per hour, for an instance that stays running between jobs
Per second of training, with the machine torn down after
questions.explanation: SageMaker provisions the machine, runs the script, streams logs, then tears it down. You pay per second of training, not for an idle instance. Endpoints are the service that bills continuously.

refLinks.label: §26.2.2 SageMaker: The ML Compute and Orchestration Layer

questions.prompt: How does SageMaker Feature Store stop training/serving skew?
options: It stores the trained model next to its features, so they load together.
It retrains the model whenever the served features drift away from the training features.
One feature computation feeds both the online store and the offline training store.
It blocks any feature that isn't present in both training and serving data.
questions.explanation: One computation feeds both stores, so train-time and serve-time features can't quietly diverge. That is the managed form of Chapter 24's shared pipeline fix. Feature Store doesn't retrain models or block features.

refLinks.label: §26.2.2 SageMaker: The ML Compute and Orchestration Layer

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter call SageMaker Pipelines narrower than a general orchestrator like Airflow?
options: It runs only on a laptop, not in the cloud.
It can't run conditional steps, so gates must be coded by hand.
It can only run one pipeline per account.
It only orchestrates ML steps, which makes it more opinionated by design.
questions.explanation: Pipelines is a versioned DAG of process, train, evaluate and conditionally register steps. It is narrower because it is built only for ML. Conditional registration is one of its core steps, so it does support gates.

refLinks.label: §26.2.2 SageMaker: The ML Compute and Orchestration Layer

questions.prompt: A customer runs its app on EC2, S3 and RDS but no SageMaker service. Is it "using SageMaker"?
options: No. SageMaker is AWS's ML platform, not a synonym for doing ML on AWS.
Yes. Any ML on AWS goes through SageMaker by default.
Yes, because S3 is part of SageMaker.
No, because SageMaker requires its own separate AWS account and billing.
questions.explanation: The chapter says this is often confused. A customer can run entirely on AWS without touching SageMaker. S3 is the foundation SageMaker reads from, not part of SageMaker. No separate account is needed.

questions.prompt: Why does S3 being the foundation matter in the lock-in conversation?
options: S3 data can only be read by SageMaker, which locks the customer in for good.
Data stays in a portable format even if compute later moves off SageMaker.
S3 is free, so storage cost never enters the decision.
S3 keeps a copy of every model in every region automatically.
questions.explanation: SageMaker reads and writes S3 directly instead of moving data into a proprietary store. So the data stays portable. The lock-in risk sits in Pipelines, Registry and Endpoints, not in the data.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the chapter say live in S3 in the AWS ML stack? Select all that apply.
options: Feature Store's low-latency online store
Training data
Feature Store's offline data
Pipeline outputs
Model artefacts
questions.explanation: The chapter lists training data, model artefacts, pipeline outputs and offline feature store data. The online store is the low-latency side for real-time inference, separate from the S3-backed offline store.

refLinks.label: §26.2.2 SageMaker: The ML Compute and Orchestration Layer

questions.prompt: What is Bedrock?
options: A GPU instance type for hosting open-weight models yourself
A service for training your own foundation model from scratch on SageMaker's managed GPUs
A managed vector database for retrieval
One API for calling pretrained models from several providers, with nothing to host
questions.explanation: Bedrock calls someone else's pretrained models (Claude, Titan, Llama and others) through one unified API. It is the managed alternative to hosting your own transformer. It is not a training service, a vector database or an instance type.

questions.prompt: What does a team give up by choosing Bedrock over hosting its own transformer?
options: Data portability, because every prompt and response must be stored inside Bedrock
Control over model internals, for zero infrastructure and a per-token bill
The ability to send more than one message per request
Access to any model but Titan
questions.explanation: The chapter says the trade is the same shape as SageMaker Endpoints against hand-hosted FastAPI: less control, no infrastructure, and per-token pricing. Bedrock offers several providers' models.

questions.prompt: A Bedrock call fails with AccessDeniedException. The IAM policy looks correct. What is the usual cause?
options: Bedrock only works in us-west-2.
The model hasn't been enabled for this account and region in the console yet.
The IAM role needs AmazonSageMakerFullAccess.
The request body is missing the anthropic_version field that Bedrock expects.
questions.explanation: Procedure 26.4's common mistake: model access must be enabled per model in the console before the first call. A malformed body gives a validation error, not access denied. Full SageMaker access is the over-broad grant the chapter warns against.

questions.prompt: Why does Listing 26.3 end with predictor.delete_endpoint()?
options: Deleting frees the model artefact in S3 for the next training job.
The endpoint can't return predictions until the call is made.
Endpoints bill continuously until deleted, whether called or not.
SageMaker requires it before the training job's logs are released.
questions.explanation: Unlike Training Jobs, billed per second of compute, real-time endpoints bill all the time. Leaving one up after a demo is the procedure's common mistake. Deleting the endpoint doesn't touch the S3 artefact.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with attaching AmazonSageMakerFullAccess to every role?
options: It expires after 24 hours, so jobs fail overnight.
It grants far more than a training job needs, which is risky outside a sandbox.
It costs extra per role per month.
It blocks access to S3 buckets, so the training job can't read any of its input data.
questions.explanation: Procedure 26.1 scopes permissions to what a job needs: S3 actions on one bucket and the specific SageMaker actions. The full-access policy is the convenient shortcut the chapter warns against outside a sandbox.

questions.prompt: In Listing 26.1, why does the S3 statement list both arn:aws:s3:::my-ml-bucket and arn:aws:s3:::my-ml-bucket/*?
options: ListBucket acts on the bucket, while GetObject and PutObject act on its objects.
The second line is a backup in case the first is mistyped.
The wildcard grants access to every bucket in the account.
SageMaker needs two copies of each permission, one per availability zone, for redundancy.
questions.explanation: In IAM, s3:ListBucket is a bucket-level action and needs the bucket ARN. Object actions need the object ARN pattern, bucket/*. The wildcard covers objects in this one bucket, not every bucket.

questions.prompt: After estimator.fit() in Listing 26.2, what does estimator.model_data hold?
options: The training job's logs
The training data, loaded into memory
The endpoint URL for real-time predictions
The s3:// path to the trained model.tar.gz
questions.explanation: The listing's comment says it is the s3:// path to model.tar.gz. Training output lands in S3, consistent with S3 as the foundation. The endpoint only exists after deploy().

questions.prompt: Which are the four axes the chapter uses to advise on SageMaker versus open source? Select all that apply.
options: Existing AWS footprint
Multi-cloud or portability requirements
Team size and platform maturity
Which programming language the team prefers
Cost model
questions.explanation: The chapter names those four axes. Language preference isn't one of them. SageMaker runs Python scripts like the ones built in earlier chapters.

refLinks.label: §26.2.4 Advising a Customer: The Actual SA Judgment Call

questions.prompt: When does the chapter say self-managed infrastructure can be cheaper than managed services?
options: At low, variable volume
At very high, steady-state volume
When the customer is new to AWS
When the team has no MLOps engineer
questions.explanation: Per-second managed billing is often cheaper at low or variable volume. Self-managed clusters can win at very high, steady volume, where dedicated hardware is used all the time. A team with no MLOps engineer benefits more from managed services.

refLinks.label: §26.2.4 Advising a Customer: The Actual SA Judgment Call

questions.prompt: In the trade-offs table, where does self-hosted open source clearly beat AWS-managed?
options: Operational burden
Time to first production model
Portability and customisation depth
Cost at low and variable training volume
questions.explanation: Open source is portable to any cloud or on-prem and gives full control of every layer. Managed wins on time to first model, operational burden, and cost at low or variable volume.

questions.prompt: A customer has a hard requirement to stay cloud-agnostic. What does that mean for SageMaker?
options: It means SageMaker can be used for training only.
It has no effect, because the four axes are averaged into one score.
It favours SageMaker, since S3 data is portable.
It rules SageMaker out, since its core services run only on AWS.
questions.explanation: The chapter says a hard cloud-agnostic requirement rules SageMaker out entirely. S3 portability keeps the data movable, but the platform services don't move. The point of the worked example is that hard constraints are not averaged.

refLinks.label: §26.2.4 Advising a Customer: The Actual SA Judgment Call

questions.prompt: Why is SageMaker close to an unambiguous recommendation for Customer A?
options: The startup is regulated, so it must use a managed service.
The team already runs Kubernetes, which SageMaker requires.
SageMaker is always cheaper than open source for startups of any size.
All four axes point the same way, so there is nothing to trade off.
questions.explanation: Customer A is a 6-person team with no MLOps engineer, already on AWS, with no multi-cloud need and low, variable volume. Every axis favours managed. There is no regulatory driver and no Kubernetes in the description.

questions.prompt: For Customer B, which axis decides the question on its own?
options: Team size. Sixty people is above the cut-off for managed services.
Existing footprint. They aren't AWS-exclusive, so they can't use AWS.
Portability. The multi-cloud requirement is a hard constraint that rules SageMaker out.
Cost. At their steady volume self-hosting is cheaper, which outweighs the other three axes.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the multi-cloud requirement rules SageMaker out structurally, regardless of the other three axes. Cost and team size lean the same way, but they are trade-offs, not constraints. The footprint axis is called a wash.

questions.prompt: What general method does the chapter draw from the two customers?
options: Check for any hard constraint first, then weigh the remaining trade-offs.
Start with cost, since the other axes follow from it.
Score each axis from 1 to 5 and recommend whichever side has the higher total.
Recommend managed services by default, and only change if the customer objects.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the call is not a scorecard averaged across four dimensions, but a check for hard constraints first, then a trade-off analysis for what's left. A scorecard could let three soft factors outvote one that rules an option out.

questions.prompt: A 12-person team with one MLOps engineer is already on AWS, has no portability requirement, and trains a large model continuously at steady high volume. How should an SA frame the advice?
options: Self-hosting is ruled out, because the team is already on AWS.
The axes cancel, so either choice is equally good and no analysis is needed.
SageMaker is ruled out, because steady high training volume is a hard constraint, like a multi-cloud rule.
No hard constraint applies, so price both: team and footprint lean managed, steady volume may not.
questions.explanation: Following the chapter's method, first check for hard constraints. There are none, since cost and footprint are trade-offs, not rules. Then weigh: small team and AWS footprint lean managed, and steady high volume is where self-managed clusters can win. The answer depends on the numbers, so price both.

refLinks.label: §26.2.4 Advising a Customer: The Actual SA Judgment Call

bookExercises.prompt: Match each of these open-source tools to its SageMaker equivalent: (a) self-hosted MLflow; (b) FastAPI + Docker; (c) Airflow.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) SageMaker's managed MLflow / SageMaker Model Registry. (b) SageMaker Endpoints (real-time) / Batch Transform (batch). (c) SageMaker Pipelines.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in one sentence why SageMaker Training Jobs are typically cheaper than running the same training on an always-on EC2 instance.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: SageMaker Training Jobs bill per second of actual training compute and tear the instance down automatically when the job finishes, while an always-on EC2 instance keeps billing whether or not it's actively training. For anything less than continuous, round-the-clock training, the ephemeral managed job avoids paying for idle compute.

bookExercises.prompt: Using this chapter's four advising axes (team maturity, portability, cost model, existing footprint), score a hypothetical 15-person team with moderate AWS usage and no regulatory constraints, and state whether any single axis would override the others the way Customer B's portability requirement did.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A 15-person team with moderate AWS usage and no regulatory constraints: team maturity is a moderate lean toward managed (some platform capability exists but likely not a dedicated MLOps function at 15 people). Portability is a non-factor since there's no regulatory constraint. Cost model is roughly neutral at moderate, likely variable volume. Existing AWS footprint gives a moderate time-to-value advantage. No single axis is a hard override here the way Customer B's portability requirement was. This is a genuine multi-factor trade-off needing real weighing, most likely landing toward managed given three of four axes lean that way, but without the "structurally rules it out" clarity of a hard constraint.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 26.3, explain what happens to billing if `predictor.delete_endpoint()` is never called after a one-off demo that used the endpoint for five minutes.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Without calling `delete_endpoint()`, the endpoint keeps running and billing continuously, per hour, not per request, indefinitely after the five-minute demo ends, until someone notices and deletes it manually. This is exactly this chapter's "surprise bill after a demo" failure mode. A five-minute use case can silently accumulate hours or days of billed endpoint uptime with zero actual inference traffic.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer says "we're on AWS, so we should use SageMaker for everything." Using this chapter's How This Connects section, write the two or three sentences you'd say back.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Being on AWS doesn't automatically mean SageMaker is the right choice for every piece. SageMaker is AWS's opinionated ML platform, not a synonym for 'doing ML on AWS.' The advising framework in this chapter is about weighing team maturity, portability needs, cost model, and existing footprint for each specific workload, not defaulting to 'we're on AWS, so use the AWS-native option' without checking whether it's actually the better fit here."

bookExercises.prompt: A customer with a hard multi-cloud regulatory requirement asks whether SageMaker Pipelines could still work "just for the AWS parts of our workload." Using this chapter's Customer B analysis, explain why portability requirements typically need to be evaluated for the whole pipeline, not service-by-service.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Portability requirements typically need whole-pipeline evaluation, because a "just the AWS parts" split creates a hidden dependency. If the SageMaker-hosted piece becomes load-bearing (e.g. the pipeline orchestration or model registry), migrating off AWS later means re-architecting that piece under pressure, defeating the point of the multi-cloud requirement in the first place. A genuine multi-cloud posture usually means every piece needs to be portable, not just most of them, since the whole point of the regulatory requirement is avoiding a single point of vendor lock-in anywhere in the critical path.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the AWS Well-Architected Framework's Machine Learning Lens. Identify one consideration it raises that this chapter's four-axis advising framework does not explicitly name, and explain where it would fit into the framework.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. The AWS Well-Architected Framework's ML Lens typically raises considerations like model governance/auditability requirements and disaster-recovery/business-continuity planning in more explicit detail than this chapter's four-axis framework does. These would fit naturally under the "cost model" and "team maturity" axes respectively, or could be treated as a fifth axis specific to regulated industries where audit trails and DR posture are themselves hard constraints, similar to how Customer B's portability requirement functioned as an override.
